title: The Central Bank Balance-Sheet Trilemma
summary: The Federal Reserve's balance sheet expanded from approximately $800 billion (6% of GDP) in December 2005 to roughly $6.5 trillion (21% of GDP) in December 2025, driven by QE programs and a 2019 shift to an ample-reserves operating framework. The paper introduces a "balance sheet trilemma" framework: central banks can achieve only two of three goals simultaneously—small balance sheet, low short-term rate volatility, and limited market intervention. The Fed concluded balance sheet reduction on December 1, 2025, and announced reserve management purchases on December 10, 2025, to maintain ample reserves.
key_points: The Fed's balance sheet grew from ~$800 billion (6% of GDP) in 2005 to ~$6.5 trillion (21% of GDP) in 2025, reflecting QE programs and the 2019 shift to ample-reserves framework
The balance sheet trilemma states central banks can only achieve two of three goals: small balance sheet, low short-term rate volatility, or limited market intervention
As reserves fall relative to outstanding Treasuries, money-market rate sensitivity rises - small shocks translate to larger rate movements
Supply-side drivers of reserve volatility include Treasury General Account (TGA), ON RRP, and foreign repo pool movements
Demand-side drivers include large payment flows, quarter-end effects, and unpredictable liquidity needs

Tradeoffs of a large balance sheet include crowding out private credit intermediation; tradeoffs of small balance sheet include higher money-market volatility and need for frequent central bank interventions
The Fed concluded active balance sheet reduction on December 1, 2025, and began reserve management purchases on December 10, 2025
why_it_matters: This FEDS Notes research provides a conceptual framework for understanding the Fed's ongoing operational challenges as it navigates post-QT positioning. Market participants monitoring reserve adequacy and potential money-market stress should understand that even small reserve buffers amplify rate volatility. The trilemma framework helps explain why the Fed cannot simultaneously minimize its market footprint, maintain rate stability, and avoid frequent operations—any two goals require sacrificing the third. This directly informs expectations about future Fed operations and potential market plumbing risks.
market_structure_context: The paper directly addresses Fed operations and market plumbing: it documents how reserve scarcity amplifies repo rate sensitivity to TGA changes, Treasury issuance, quarter-ends, and foreign repo pool shifts. The empirical relationship between normalized reserves and rate volatility provides a quantitative framework for monitoring money-market stress. Figures show TGCR-ON RRP spread sensitivity and volatility rising as reserves decline relative to Treasuries. The Fed's December 2025 shift to reserve management purchases reflects recognition of these dynamics.
